channel.title: Historical Materialism
channel.description: Latest articles from Historical Materialism journal, via CrossRef

item.title: Labour as the Form of the Body: Fleshing out Marx’s Aristotelianism
item.description: Author(s): Ben Suriano — This essay aims to reconstruct Marx’s normative account of the labouring body in a non-reductive, historical materialist way by drawing out underexplored Aristotelian aspects in his work. It points out problems in both critical theory and certain historical materialist accounts of labour and the body insofar as they neglect this influence. Marx’s Aristotelian trajectory indicates labour as the normative form of the body beyond any monological subject or mere utility because the sensuously social body dialectically emerges as the content and new end for labour. Labour is then understood as the praxis of community-making that further makes its body. Yet, this praxis is only intelligible for Marx according to an emergent telos of beauty whose horizon of mutual flourishing necessarily includes the whole of nature in a way that challenges capitalism’s narrow anthropocentrism without sacrificing the distinctively human.
item.author: Ben Suriano

item.title: The Althusserian Transformation of Philosophy
item.description: Author(s): José Luis Moreno Pestaña — In this text I reconstruct the thinking behind Althusser’s work to define philosophy, which culminated in his 1976 presentation at the Granada conference. I start by exploring how philosophy exploits and reorganises other forms of knowledge and social practices by means of an analysis of Althusser’s works in the later part of the 1960s. Subsequently, I examine and outline the debates on how the mode of production affects the superstructure. I then turn to the positions of Althusser’s interlocutor at the Granada conference, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, who defended the idea that philosophy was affected by the mode of production. Finally, I examine the implications of the changes and innovations in Althusserian thought set out at the conference for the conception of philosophy.
item.author: José Luis Moreno Pestaña

item.title: Special Issue on Strategy
item.description: Author(s): Josep Maria Antentas, Panagiotis Sotiris — In a period marked by the inability of all variants of the Left to overcome the burden of defeat and fragmentation, of constant vacillations between reformism and sectarianism, this special issue of Historical Materialism attempts to reopen questions of strategy.
item.author: Josep Maria Antentas, Panagiotis Sotiris

item.title: Structure and Method of the Critique of Political Economy
item.description: Author(s): Ehrenfried Galander, Axel Rüdiger — With the initial publication of his main economic work in 1859, Marx formulated his programme for an analysis of the bourgeois economy in the following order: capital, landed property, wage labour; state, foreign trade, world market. It was not until the 1920s and 1950s that Henryk Grossman and Roman Rosdolsky discussed whether the content of ‘Capital’ was based on a change in Marx’s structural plan. Important impulses for this discussion in the GDR , the FRG and the Soviet Union came in the following years from the advancing publication of the MEGA ² since 1976. We pay particular attention to the work of Wolfgang Jahn’s research group at the University of Halle. At the heart of this was and is the question of whether methodological and/or substantive breaks can be recognised in Marx’s critique of political economy that point to a change in his conceptions of planning. We deny this with reference to the continuity of his dialectical method of antithetical determination.
item.author: Ehrenfried Galander, Axel Rüdiger

item.title: The Origins of Neoliberal Authoritarianism
item.description: Author(s): Daniel McLoughlin — This essay intervenes in contemporary debates around neoliberalism and its relationship to both authoritarianism and social democracy. It does so by reconstructing the debate on Thatcherism that took place between Stuart Hall and Bob Jessop in the 1980s. Both authors provide materialist analyses of Thatcherism that point to important continuities, at the level of both political economy and authoritarian political technique, between her hegemonic project and late-stage social democracy. I argue that this provides an antidote to the social democratic nostalgia that is the potential product of the ways that neoliberalism is frequently theorised in the contemporary literature. While both thinkers highlight these continuities, they are more obviousin Jessop’s institutional approach to hegemony than in Hall’s analysis of Thatcher’s ideology.
item.author: Daniel McLoughlin

item.title: Integrating Finance and Social Reproduction: Capital, Labour-Power, and Working-Class Formation
item.author: Sean Kazuo Isaacs

item.title: Racialised Gradients of Human Value and Marx’s Working Day, Today
item.description: Author(s): Anthony F. Peressini — This paper reconsiders the ‘working day’ discussion in chapter ten of Capital and how it centres two parameters in the generation and appropriation of surplus value. The first parameter is the cost of labour-power paid by the capitalist and the second is the time that the worker must yield to the capitalist: the ‘length of the working day’. The first parameter represents the amount of pay required to keep the worker alive and able to work. Marx understood it as a lower limit below which capitalism would cease to function. This paper argues that, while analytically coherent, this understanding of a lower limit runs contrary to many ways that actual historical capitalism has found to exploit the working class. Capitalism regularly exceeds this limit and, in this sense, hyper-exploits. What we find instead of a limit are racialised gradients of human value – generated and fostered by capitalism – in which there are regular and persisting areas of hyper-exploitation with devalued racialised gendered workers. Supplemented by the notion of gradients of human value, Marx’s two-parameter account with its unifying analytic of time, in particular human-time, neatly encompasses the phenomenon of hyper-exploitation and provides an incisive analysis of today’s capitalist exploitation.
item.author: Anthony F. Peressini

item.title: Desire Beyond Value: On Reproduction, Queerness, and (Anti-) Fascism
item.description: Author(s): Alexander Stoffel — This paper argues that both fascist and queer politics are animated by the erotics of transgression: the pleasure that derives from the act of violating normative boundaries concerning gender, sexuality, and the body. Yet while fascism eroticises the restoration of hierarchies of human value, queerness eroticises the destruction of those hierarchical classifications. Against economistic and orthodox psychoanalytic accounts, this paper argues that the erotic charge of transgression emerges from capitalism’s devaluation of embodied needs and desires. By hierarchising needs according to their representability within the terms of value production, capitalism produces a historically specific distinction between profitable and unprofitable needs. Because the body resists full subsumption, many of our bodily needs, desires and capacities are abandoned by capital and can often only be met, if at all, through relations of dependency in the reproductive sphere. It is around this site of abandonment that erotic fantasies of transgression cluster.
item.author: Alexander Stoffel

item.title: Rearguard Politics: Rethinking Political Leadership From the Back
item.description: Author(s): Lukas Slothuus — Which kinds of leadership are appropriate for emancipatory politics? Moving beyond a dichotomy of vanguardism and horizontalism, I advance rearguardism. Supplementing vanguardism, rearguardism involves defensive leadership and legitimation of existing movements, protecting these from attacks by dominant forces and actively propagating their struggles without co-opting or directing these from the front. I first outline vanguardism, focusing on the work of Vladimir Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg. I then reconstruct the most prominent account of rearguardism, by Boaventura de Sousa Santos, before arguing that his account is too dematerialised and confined to an epistemic realm. I therefore reformulate a different vision of rearguardism by turning to Antonio Gramsci.
item.author: Lukas Slothuus

item.title: Labour Law, Strategy, and the Structural Critique of Capitalism
item.description: Author(s): Zoe Adams — This article argues that UK labour law scholarship has failed to engage sufficiently with Marxian insights about the nature and basis of employer power and exploitation, and about the limits of law as a means through which to overcome them. As a result, it lacks a strategic orientation, commitment to structural change and theoretical foundations that would enable it to overcome the causes of the problems against which labour law is traditionally directed. The article begins by elaborating a Marxian inspired account of employer-power and the associated problem of exploitation, teasing out its strategic implications. It then explores a range of Marxian contributions to the question of the role of law in the struggle for structural change. It then uses insights from this discussion to explain the potentially important role that labour law scholarship might play in advancing such struggles, before exploring whether UK labour law scholarship has ever embraced such a role for itself in practice. Concluding that UK labour law scholarship has never embraced such a role, the article suggests how UK labour law scholarship might more effectively perform such a strategic role today.
item.author: Zoe Adams

item.title: Gaining Power and Using It: the Promise and Limits of Socialism in Mouffe and Piketty
item.description: Author(s): John Grant, Simon Choat — Throughout Western democracies, the left remains in political purgatory and without a road towards political power. We examine Chantal Mouffe’s strategy for achieving a left populism with socialist characteristics, followed by Thomas Piketty’s program for ‘participatory socialism’. We highlight the admirable details they offer about alliance politics and transforming property relations. Nevertheless, we argue for why they cannot realise in practice what they hope to achieve, in part because of their respective convictions about the autonomy of the political. Mouffe’s treatment of economic and political liberalism, and her misreading of class relations and neoliberal oligarchy, leave her politics within a liberal capitalist orbit. Piketty’s work is overly idealist and insufficiently critical, and his proposed changes to capitalist and political institutions are too narrow. Their merits notwithstanding, socialist strategy must go beyond Mouffe and Piketty.
item.author: John Grant, Simon Choat

item.title: ‘Seize the Time’ – Abolition & Revolution at the Crossroads
item.description: Author(s): Denis Bosseau — While abolition and revolution might appear complementary, it is not always easy to see how they can relate with each other as part of a coherent conception of emancipatory struggle, nor how such complementarity might inform political strategy. In response to this problem, the objective of this paper is to contribute to a critical reappraisal of the revolutionary heritage of abolitionist thought by drawing attention to what Joy James called ‘the revolutionary era’ of abolitionist politics of the late 1960s and early 1970s USA, focusing on the organisational politics of George Jackson who I consider to be one of the period’s most original thinkers. The claim I would like the reader to consider is that the type of vanguardism once presented by revolutionary abolitionists like George Jackson can help us to re-evaluate the political and ideological basis upon which a greater socialisation of struggles can be built today in view of the constitution of potential counter-hegemonic blocks capable of contesting the demands that capital makes on the planet and our lives. To put it in broader terms, the paper hopes to contribute to a widening of the conversation on how the question of abolition can help us rethink revolutionary politics in the twenty-first century.
item.author: Denis Bosseau

item.title: Strategy at an Impasse: Prolonged Dual Power, State Capacities and Social Reproduction Struggles
item.description: Author(s): Michael Bray — Stasis amidst crisis defines the present conjuncture, while the left seems trapped in a fractured sequence between short-lived and fundamentally constrained uprisings and electoral bids. This essay attempts to define the terrain of contemporary struggles in reference to their impasses, especially as these relate to transformations in capitalist nation-states. Tracing the limits of opposed strategic poles – a strong ‘protective’ state and ‘prolonged’ forms of dual power – it situates their common turn to social reproduction struggles and criticises their common presupposition: that states have abandoned core aspects of social reproduction, opening new paths for resistance. Instead we have ‘organised abandonment’: the developing, if still contradictory, integration of state capacities and international capital, extending into new modalities of social reproduction. State capacities have come to be structured in ways that impose impasses on traditional aims of working-class autonomy. In this light, the key strategic question is how we can conceive of an ascending sequence of struggles.
item.author: Michael Bray

item.title: On Strategy: Thinking with the Military
item.description: Author(s): Josep Maria Antentas — This article discusses the concept of strategy and how contemporary military thinking can contribute to strategy from below. First it discusses the military lineages of the term ‘strategy’. Second, the evolution of its meaning and its entry into the labour movement. Third, the relationship with ‘tactics’. Fourth, it analyses the concept of ‘operational art’ and explores how it can be used outside the military field. Fifth, it reviews some key debates on contemporary military strategy to enrich the understanding of strategy. Sixth, it explores new military analogies based on the concepts of asymmetric, unrestricted and hybrid warfare. Finally, it considers the term ‘grand strategy’ to assess its value for strategy from below.
item.author: Josep Maria Antentas

item.title: Towards a Communist Strategy of Reappropriation
item.description: Author(s): Isabelle Garo — Is the strategic question back on the agenda? Construed as awareness of the relative autonomy of political intervention, its return presents a challenge. Amid persistent but fragile neo-liberal hegemony, vigorous but scattered social struggles, and alternatives that are theoretically developed but disconnected from real conditions, strategy involves reinventing the ways and means of an effective break with the capitalist organisation of the world. Reconsidering the classical question of property in conjunction with the production and reproduction of labour-power, I shall endeavour to show that the perspective of reappropriation can unify existing mobilisations without infringing their autonomy or forsaking their aggressive political structuration. To this end, I shall suggest a critical analysis of the theses of Negri and Hardt on the common, in as much as they invite us to re-read Marx from the political and strategic angle of social reappropriation as both means and end of collective and individual emancipation.
item.author: Isabelle Garo
